content.text:
The single eccentric planet in H1 does not fully explain the data: the leftover scatter is 6.70 m/s, well above the 3.8 m/s limit, even though no single leftover signal is significant.

**Best fit: F1** (hypothesis H1, period allowed to move ±10%). It is stored in the ledger.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Period | 184.80 d (start 178.6 d; ±10% search bound is ~160.7–196.5 d, so not on the bound) |
| K (velocity semi-amplitude) | 37.43 m/s |
| Eccentricity | 0.403 |
| ω (argument of periastron) | 3.416 rad |
| RMS scatter of residuals | **6.70 m/s, limit 3.77 m/s → fails** |
| Reduced χ² | 7.97 (target ≈ 1) |
| BIC | 628.9, lower is better; this is 2898 lower than the no-planet model |
| Flags | none (period not stuck on a bound, eccentricity not extreme) |
| Observations | 56 |

I didn't refit with a wider period range or register a corrected hypothesis, because the fit raised no flags.

**Residual periodogram for F1:**
- Strongest peak: **22.69 d, false-alarm probability 2.6%**, above the 1% threshold, so not significant.
- Next: 45.54 d (false-alarm probability 5.0%). The tool marks 22.69 d and 45.54 d as harmonics of each other (45.5 ≈ 2 × 22.7).
- 30.70 d (false-alarm probability 12%). All other peaks have a false-alarm probability above 50%.
- The 88 d harmonic seen before the fit is no longer among the top residual peaks. That fits the expectation that the eccentric orbit causes it.

**For the PI:** the eccentric orbit accounts for the 178.6 d signal and its 88 d harmonic. But the scatter limit fails clearly, and the 22.7/45.5 d pair is close to significant, so H1 alone is probably not enough. Two ways to test this: the BIC comparison with H2 (178.6 + 88.1 d), or a hypothesis with an extra planet near 22.7 or 45.5 d. I haven't added any planets myself.
